content: The Cercozoa are a diverse group of protists that include most amoeboid and flagellated organisms which feed using thin, thread-like extensions of their cytoplasm called filose pseudopodia. These pseudopodia may be localized to specific regions of the cell surface, but unlike many other protozoa, Cercozoa lack a true cytostome, or mouth structure, for ingestion. Cercozoa exhibit a wide range of morphological forms, making them challenging to define based on structural characteristics alone. However, genetic studies strongly support their classification as a unified group. They are closely related to Foraminifera and Radiolaria, which are amoeboid organisms typically characterized by their intricate shells. Together, these groups form a larger clade known as the Rhizaria. Among the best-known members of the Cercozoa are the Euglyphids, which are filose amoebae that construct shells from siliceous scales or plates. These organisms are commonly found in soils, nutrient-rich aquatic environments, and on aquatic plants. Other filose amoebae within the group, such as the Tectofilosids and Gromia, produce organic shells. Historically, these organisms were grouped with the Euglyphids under the classification Testaceafilosia. However, this grouping is not monophyletic, though most studied members are either part of or closely related to the Cercozoa, sharing similarities with shell-bearing flagellates. Another notable subgroup within the Cercozoa is the Chlorarachniophytes, which are unique amoebae that form a reticulating network. These organisms are distinguished by the presence of chloroplasts, which are believed to have originated from an engulfed green alga. The chloroplasts in Chlorarachniophytes are surrounded by four membranes and retain a vestigial nucleus, known as a nucleomorph. This feature has made them a subject of significant interest in studies on the endosymbiotic origins of organelles. Other prominent cercozoans include the Cercomonads, which are common soil-dwelling flagellates, and the Phaeodarea, marine protozoa that were previously classified as Radiolarians. Additionally, three groups traditionally considered Heliozoans—Dimorphids, Desmothoracids, and Gymnosphaerids—are now recognized as part of the Cercozoa. The classification and composition of the Cercozoa remain an area of active research. Some basal members of the group may include parasitic organisms such as the Phytomyxea and Ascetosporea, as well as the shell-bearing amoeba Gromia, though certain phylogenetic trees place these closer to the Foraminifera. The Spongomonads were once included in the Cercozoa but are now more commonly associated with the Amoebozoa. Furthermore, several small and poorly understood groups of protozoans are tentatively classified as Cercozoa, and it is likely that additional obscure genera will be identified as cercozoans with further study.
